content: The updated recommendations for the treatment of adolescents and children with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection emphasize the use of direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens, which have revolutionized HCV management. These regimens are highly effective, require short courses of oral treatment, and have excellent safety profiles. The primary goal of HCV treatment is to prevent advanced liver disease and extrahepatic complications by eliminating viremia, a marker of active infection. Additionally, treatment reduces the risk of transmission and improves the quality of life for patients. Since 2017, DAAs have been approved for adolescents aged 12 years and older, and some regimens have been extended to younger children. The first DAA regimen approved for younger children was the fixed-dose combination of sofosbuvir and ledipasvir (SOF + LDV). Other approved regimens include sofosbuvir and ribavirin (SOF + RBV) for genotypes 2 and 3, glecaprevir and pibrentasvir (GLC + PIB) as a pangenotypic option, and sofosbuvir and velpatasvir (SOF + VEL), which is also pangenotypic. The combination of sofosbuvir, velpatasvir, and voxilaprevir (SOF + VEL + VOX) has been approved for adolescents aged 12–17 years. Additionally, the use of sofosbuvir and daclatasvir (SOF + DCV) has been reported in observational studies, demonstrating safety and efficacy, though it has not been submitted for regulatory approval. A systematic review and meta-analysis conducted in 2020 identified 39 eligible studies involving 1,796 children and adolescents with chronic HCV infection. The pooled data showed a 100% sustained virological response at 12 weeks post-treatment (SVR12) among those who completed treatment. Headache and fatigue were the most common adverse events, while serious adverse events were rare. The study aimed to summarize the scientific evidence on DAA treatment for chronic HCV infection in children and adolescents, updating previous reviews. The research questions focused on identifying appropriate DAA regimens for different age groups: adolescents (12–18 years), older children (6–11 years), and young children (3–5 years). The primary outcome of interest was SVR12, a well-established measure of cure and viral clearance. The review included randomized clinical trials (RCTs), non-RCTs, and observational studies. Due to the high efficacy of DAAs, placebo-controlled trials are no longer considered ethical, and few studies directly compare different DAA regimens. Regulatory approvals for some regimens have been based on uncontrolled trials. SVR12 is considered an interpretable outcome even without a comparison group, as spontaneous clearance of HCV is rare. The search strategy involved PubMed and Embase databases, as well as conference abstracts from major hepatology and pediatric societies. Screening and data extraction were conducted independently by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved through discussion. The risk of bias was assessed using modified Cochrane tools, considering factors such as participant selection, intervention misclassification, and missing data. For efficacy analysis, the proportion of participants achieving SVR12 was calculated using various definitions, including intention-to-treat (ITT), modified ITT (mITT), and per-protocol (PP) analyses. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to account for participants lost to follow-up, assuming them as either treatment failures or excluding them from the numerator. In summary, the updated recommendations highlight the transformative impact of DAAs in treating chronic HCV infection in children and adolescents, with a focus on achieving high cure rates, ensuring safety, and improving patient outcomes.
